nameStory: The white-striped black moth gets its straightforward name from its distinctive appearance - bold white stripes cutting across dark wings like racing stripes on a midnight canvas. This no-nonsense name perfectly captures what catches your eye first when you spot one of these striking moths.
description: The white-striped black moth is a small, elegant member of the geometer moth family, known for their distinctive looping caterpillar walk. Adults have a wingspan of about 20-25mm (roughly the size of a quarter), making them one of the smaller moths you'll encounter. True to their name, they display contrasting dark wings marked with crisp white stripes that make them unmistakable when spotted.

idTips.label: Wing Pattern
idTips.description: Bold white stripes run across dark brown to black wings, creating a striking contrast that's visible even in dim light

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small wingspan of 20-25mm - about the diameter of a quarter when wings are spread

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Typical geometer moth build with a slender body and wings held horizontally when at rest

idTips.label: Flight Period
idTips.description: Active from April through September, with peak activity during warm summer evenings

idTips.label: Resting Position
idTips.description: Often found resting on tree bark or walls during the day with wings spread flat against the surface

habitat: Look for white-striped black moths in areas where jewelweed (wild touch-me-not) grows abundantly, as this is their caterpillar host plant. They're commonly found near streams, woodland edges, and shaded garden areas where these moisture-loving plants thrive. You'll often spot them around porch lights or windows at night, drawn in from nearby wooded areas.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in April, with early individuals appearing on warm evenings near outdoor lights.
seasonality.summer: Peak flight season with moths most active and visible. Look for them at dusk around lights or resting on tree bark during hot afternoons.
seasonality.fall: Flight season continues into early fall, with the last stragglers typically seen in September before cold weather ends their activity.
seasonality.winter: Inactive season - the species overwinters in a dormant stage, waiting for spring's return.

funFact: The caterpillars of white-striped black moths feed exclusively on jewelweed, the same plant whose crushed stems provide natural relief from poison ivy and stinging nettle - making these moths inadvertent partners with one of nature's best first-aid plants!
confusionNotes: The bold white stripes on dark wings make this species quite distinctive among New England moths. While other small dark moths exist, few have such crisp, contrasting white markings, making misidentification unlikely.
contextualKnowledge: This moth belongs to the Geometridae family, whose name comes from Greek meaning 'earth measurers' - a reference to how their caterpillars appear to measure the ground as they move in their characteristic inchworm fashion.
compareHints: As the only Trichodezia species regularly found in New England, white-striped black moths are unique in their genus here. They can be distinguished from other small dark geometers by their particularly bold white striping and consistent size - many similar moths either lack the crisp white markings or are noticeably larger or smaller.
